The loop ran on Sonnet, which may weigh less per dollar than Opus.

method: Reproduced the counts from scratch/failmodes/turns.jsonl. The 12,768 turns are the 'cont_normal' turns with 1 tool call or fewer: 12,255 Codex and 513 Claude, out of 22,613 turns. I then re-scanned the raw Codex rollouts for all 12,255 Codex turns in that set, reading task_complete, turn_aborted, response_item assistant messages and timestamps. I recomputed turn duration as the time from task_started to task_complete or turn_aborted. I checked the streak-length histogram against the 'continuation turn #N of M' text in the prompt, and checked TurnPrompt in src/lib/aiur/agent_runner/turn_prompt.ex. The final messages were re-classified with two different regex orderings. Scripts and output are in scratch/verify-agents-01-interpret/.
note:
The main count is right, and the turns are genuine waits. But several of the supporting figures come from how they were measured.
(1) DURATION. The extractor ends a Codex turn at the last event before the next task_started. That event is usually thread_settings_applied, which is written when the next run resumes the thread, often hours later. Example: aiur#1492 ended its turn in 3 s, with task_complete at 09:17:26, but it was counted as 6,932 s. Measured to task_complete or turn_aborted, the no-op turns add up to about 20 h (19.2 h Codex + 1.0 h Claude), not 186 h. The median is 4.4 s, 99.8% are under 60 s, and the longest is 200 s. In the original figure, 143 turns (1.1%) carried 137 of the 186 h. By the same measure, Codex turn time overall is about 518 h, not 1,694 h, so the no-op share of Codex time is about 4%.
(2) EMPTY FINAL MESSAGE. The '15.7%' bucket (2,002 turns) is mostly an extractor gap. Newer Codex versions put the final text in task_complete.last_agent_message and item_completed, not in agent_message events. 1,825 of the 1,999 Codex 'empty' turns do have a final message. Only 177 turns (1.4%) truly have none, and 135 of those are Codex 'You've hit your usage limit' errors. Those are failed turns, not waits.
(3) REASON SPLIT. With the missing messages restored, the turns still read as waits. But the split depends on the order in which the regexes are applied. With my regexes it came out as CI about 23-35%, dependency about 18-25%, review about 9-23% and decision about 2-6%. The claimed 28.4/27.8/14.2/5.6 is one ordering, not a stable result.
(4) STREAKS. Codex ran with max_turns=12: 10,652 of the continuation prompts read 'of 12'. So 618 of the 712 streaks of 10 or more are exactly 11 turns long, which is the per-run cap. 1,008 streaks end at the 'session resumed after an aiur restart' prompt, which TurnPrompt sends on any resumed re-dispatch, not only after a restart. When streaks are joined across that boundary, 227 wait loops run 20 or more turns, 63 run 50 or more, and the longest is 132. The claim gives 31. So the streak figures measure the run cap, not how long the loops last.
(5) CONCENTRATION. 96% of these turns are Codex: 63.8% of Codex turns, against 15.1% of Claude turns. Claude on aiur and archon has none. 72% fall in ISO weeks 31-32, and the top 50 of 2,442 sessions hold 76%. A 1-tool turn is usually a poll: a skill-file re-read plus a git or gh check. In 322 turns, that one exec call runs 2-4 nested tools.

method:
I wrote my own streaming extractor before I read the author's script. It is in <local-research-root>/scratch/verify-agents04/.
(1) classify.py reads the first session_meta of all 6,534 files in ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl. A file is an Aiur thread when its cwd matches `workspaces/(?:.*/)?<owner>/<repo>/<n>`. All non-primary files have a `source.subagent` object.
(2) turns.py splits each primary file into turns from `task_started` to `task_complete`/`turn_aborted`. It takes the prompt from the `user_message` event. Newer files have an `"ordinal"` field and no `user_message`, so for those it falls back to the first non-context `response_item` user message. On the 15,650 turns that have both, the two sources agree 100%. It counts tool calls (function/custom/local_shell/web_search/etc.) and sums `last_token_usage` from every `token_count` event in the turn. It keeps two sums: naive, and deduped (repeat events with the same cumulative total are skipped).
Coverage check (check.py): 0 unparsed lines out of 979,593. In-turn deduped tokens are 21.392 B and the sum of positive cumulative `total_token_usage` deltas is 21.371 B, a 0.1% difference.
(3) sum.py uses the report's no-op definition: the prompt starts with "Continuation guidance:" and contains "previous turn completed normally", and the turn has ≤1 tool call.
Commands: `python3 .../verify-agents04/classify.py && python3 .../verify-agents04/turns.py && python3 .../verify-agents04/sum.py`.
Only after this did I run a copy of the author's scratch/failmodes/noop_tokens.py. It gives the same numbers.
note:
REPRODUCED EXACTLY. My independent run gives 12,255 no-op turns in 265 primary Codex threads. The naive sum of last_token_usage.total_tokens is 2,498,613,667, identical to the claim. - Dropping repeated token_count events (same cumulative total) gives 2,487,605,257, 0.44% lower. That is well within tolerance.

ONE SUB-FIGURE IS MISLEADING. "1.68 M output plus reasoning" reproduces arithmetically: output_tokens 1,357,046 + reasoning_output_tokens 323,208 = 1,680,254. The part of the 2.4986 B total that the model generated is about 1.36 M (of which about 0.32 M is reasoning). Input is 2,496,111,230, and 1.15 M sits in zero-breakdown events.

corrected_claim: On Codex alone, 12,255 no-op continuation turns in 265 primary threads used about 2.5 billion tokens: 2,498,613,667 summed from per-event last_token_usage, or 2,487,605,257 after removing repeated token_count events. method: Code: I read src/lib/aiur/agent_runner/turn_prompt.ex (build_turn_prompt for N>1 holds the literal text) and turn_loop.ex continue_with_issue?/2. Every tracked config (aiur, archon, kevinweaver-dev and the others) sets active_states = todo, in-progress, rework, merging. ci-wait and human-review are NOT in it. ci_lifecycle.ex: transition_ci_pass and the ci-wait rewake fallback (ci_wait_rewake_minutes, default 5, also present at c24ace06 on 2026-07-30) move ci-wait to in-progress. For each 'Continuation guidance… previous turn completed normally' prompt I tracked the agent's last state-label write (--add-label or REST labels[]=). I also parsed every `gh issue view … labels` read that an agent made inside a continuation turn. I traced one case turn by turn (codex rollout 2026-07-30T06-56-24…, L211-L303). note:
What reproduces:
(1) The prompt text, and that it fires only on an active label, up to the per-run cap. Caps seen: 12 on 11,700 prompts, 8 on 1,147, 4 on 205. 783 prompts had no cap, and those runs went as high as #311.
(2) The volume of continuation prompts: I count 13,149 Codex and 688 Claude (the report says 13,544 and 688). The Codex gap is about 3% and comes from how primary threads were selected.
(3) The count of sessions that ran `gh pr checks` 5 or more times: I get 62 (56 Codex, 6 Claude). The report says 60.

What does not reproduce: "agents correctly parked in agent:ci-wait / human-review still get re-prompted".
- A ticket that carries those labels does not get this prompt. Neither label is an active state in any config.
- Agents read their labels 560 times inside continuation turns before any label edit in that turn. About 498 of those reads showed an active label. Only 3 showed a parked label alone.
- Traced case: the agent sets agent:ci-wait and confirms that label alone (14:02:29). About 6.5 minutes later the daemon's own ci-wait rewake or CI pass moves the ticket to in-progress. Then continuations #3 to #8 fire 8 seconds apart. In each one the agent runs `gh pr checks` and says it "stays in agent:ci-wait". So the re-prompts come after the daemon un-parks the ticket, and the agent never re-parks it. They do not come while it is parked.
- Other sources:
  - Agents waiting on a dependency, a review or a decision while the label is still in-progress.
  - About 47 of 97 immediate cases added ci-wait without removing in-progress. That combination resolves to in-progress.
  - Before #1940 (2026-08-16), agent:paused tickets: 1,204 prompts followed an agent-added agent:paused. That is 0 from ISO week 34 onward.
- Most prompts where the last label the agent set was ci-wait (3,713 of them) came after a restart-resume (2,674) or an <aiur:events> prompt. A resume only happens once the ticket is active again.

The "1,158 ci-wait label adds" figure: I count 1,713 real add operations (1,398 --add-label and 315 REST labels[]) across 905 sessions. The author's pattern matches any command that mentions agent:ci-wait, including removes and reads. Summed from their feature files it gives 2,832 hits, which is not 1,158 either.

The last sentence of the claim ("same root" behind the two largest items) only restates §6 of the report. It rests on this same flawed mechanism.
corrected_claim:
The daemon sends 'Continuation guidance: The previous turn completed normally, but the issue is still in an active state…' only when the re-fetched ticket state is in tracker.active_states (todo, in-progress, rework, merging). Since #1940 (2026-08-16) it also requires that the ticket is not paused. It keeps sending this up to the per-run turn cap (usually 12, sometimes 8 or 4, and some runs are uncapped), and then a new run starts.

A ticket that actually carries agent:ci-wait or agent:human-review does not get this prompt. The no-op loop happens when a waiting agent's label is active:
(a) The daemon itself moves ci-wait to in-progress, either on the 5-minute ci-wait rewake fallback or on a CI pass. The agent re-checks CI, finds it still pending, and ends the turn without re-parking. From then on every turn is a generic continuation.
(b) The agent waits on CI, a dependency, a review or a decision but leaves agent:in-progress on the ticket (or adds ci-wait without removing in-progress, which resolves to in-progress).
(c) Before 2026-08-16, the ticket was paused (1,204 prompts).

Agent self-polling is minor: 62 sessions ran `gh pr checks` 5 or more times. Agents add agent:ci-wait about 1,700 times, not 1,158. The waste therefore comes from daemon re-prompts on tickets whose label is active. It does not come from re-prompts on tickets that are still parked.

method: I pulled every command string that mentions guard-pr-deletions out of scratch/failmodes/cmds.jsonl: 3,009 strings, 2,006 from Codex exec and 1,003 from Claude Bash. I split them into guard invocations and non-invocations with a structural classifier that finds the command word of the segment and the operator that follows it (scripts and output are in scratch/verify-agents-08-interp/). A naive regex, guard-pr-deletions[^\n]*\|\s*(tail|head|grep) with no pipefail anywhere in the string, gives exactly 1,052, so this is almost certainly how the report's number was made. I then searched the raw sessions (~/.claude/projects, ~/.codex/sessions) for real runtime refusal output, meaning a line with an actual number, not source text that still contains $base_branch. For each refusal I traced what the agent did next.
note:
Two parts of the claim are measurement errors, and the conclusion is contradicted by the only direct evidence available.

(1) The 1,052 figure mixes in commands that are not the pattern it describes. About 240 of the naive matches never run the guard: they are searches or inspections such as `rg -n "guard-pr-deletions" … | head -80` (191 are rg), plus find, sed and similar. About 110 more are commands where the pipe belongs to a later command, such as `guard "$AIUR_BASE_BRANCH" && git push 2>&1 | tail -2`. That is the protected && pattern counted as masking. Only about 695 invocations pipe the guard itself into tail, head or grep.

(2) "Only protects when chained with &&" is wrong. About 764 invocations push later in the same command:
- about 353 gate the push with &&
- about 61 gate it with `set -e`
- about 350 do not gate it (about 235 through a pipe, about 110 run it sequentially without set -e, 6 through ||)

Codex agents also gate on exit_code in the JS wrapper (for example `if(r.exit_code!==0)exit()`), and a string classifier cannot see that. Some of the "echo" cases are `echo "guard exit=$?"`, which shows the status rather than hiding it.

(3) The inference from masking to "effectively advisory" does not follow. In most invocations (about 1,600 of 2,371) the push is a separate, later tool call. The agent reads the guard's output before it pushes, and the refusal text goes to stderr, so it stays visible even when stdout is piped. The raw sessions show the guard printing its pass line in 459 sessions and actually refusing in only 6. In all 6 the agent honored the refusal. It either merged the base and repaired the branch, re-ran the guard until it passed before pushing, or pushed only a rescue ref after an &&-chained guard had blocked the combined push. One of these refusals came from a command whose exit status was masked by a trailing `; echo`. The agent still read the text, re-ran the guard, and pushed only after it passed. No case shows a push going through after a refusal.

So the masking is a real but latent gap in about 350 same-command pushes. It is not an observed failure, and the bigger problem is the guard not running at all ("unknown command", 579 sessions).
corrected_claim: Of about 3,000 guard-related command strings, about 2,370 actually run the guard. About 700 of those pipe it straight into tail, head or grep without pipefail. The published 1,052 also counts about 240 `rg`/`find` searches for the string, and about 110 commands where the pipe belongs to a later `git push`. About 350 invocations push later in the same command with no exit-status gate. About 410 gate that push with `&&` (about 350) or `set -e` (about 60). In most invocations the push is a separate, later tool call made after the agent has read the guard's output. The guard's exit status therefore decides nothing only in those ~350 same-command pushes. The guard really refused in only 6 sessions, and in all 6 the agent honored the refusal (repaired the base or re-ran the guard before pushing), including once when the exit status was masked. Exit masking is a latent weakness, not evidence that the guard is advisory in practice. The observed failure is that the guard often does not run at all (unknown command in 579 sessions).
